newsitem.title: GERMANY: Bunds at risk as EMU politics eclipse politics.
newsitem.headline: Bunds at risk as EMU politics eclipse politics.

text.p: Rumblings this weekend of a softening in Germany's stance on the entry criteria for Europe's planned single currency confirmed market suspicions that politics, not economics, will drive the project through.
Economists said on Monday the key issue for Germany's government bond, or Bund, market was the extent of any political deal struck over economic and monetary union (EMU).

While finance minister Theo Waigel on Monday denied reports that Germany was shying away from strict application of EMU's starting rules, the fact he was no longer stating explicitly that the three percent deficit target must mean 3.0 percent suggested otherwise, analysts said.
Waigel switched this year from using a clear "3.0 percent" to clarify the maximum accepted public deficit level compared to gross domestic product to the less specific "three".

Under the Maastricht Treaty which set out the economic criteria a country must meet to join EMU from the start in 1999, a key requirement is to bring its fiscal deficit down to three percent of gross domestic product.

After a meeting of European finance ministers in the Netherlands this weekend, he was quoted by two British dailies on Monday as saying: "I have never nailed myself to the cross of three percent. When I said in the past 'three percent means three percent', I did not necessarily mean 3.0 percent."
Waigel later termed the newspaper reports "unfair in the highest degree".
But analysts said the message from the weekend was clear.
"The project remains on target and politics is obviously the driving force -- not economics," said Michael O'Hanlon, chief international economist at PaineWebber in London.
"And I can't help but be sceptical of Bund market performance in that context."

Germany's own efforts to meet the entry requirements for EMU are being hampered by sluggish economic growth and cripplingly high unemployment levels -- together presenting a serious threat to its own ability to meet the 3.0 percent defifit to growth ratio set out in the Maastricht Treaty.

With the so-called "Club Med" countries of Italy, Spain and Portugal keen to join the first wave of economic and monetary union (EMU) in 1999, the risk for Bunds is that a "political" interpretation of the rules to allow Germany and France in will also open the door to weaker currency members.

"The German government has been waiting for the right time to admit to the markets that yes, it looks like a political solution will be found to allow EMU to go ahead on time, with a fairly large group," said John Butler, senior fixed income analyst at WestLB bank in Duesseldorf.
"And anything that suggests that there will be a large EMU is negative for the Bund market."
For the time being, German Bunds were taking the weekend's developments in their stride, with the DTB June future trading 34 basis points higher at 99.64 by 1131 GMT.
But analysts said the fresh EMU worries would soon begin to bite in the market.

The German government seemed to be backing itself into a corner, they said, keen not to be seen to be widening the goalposts to ensure a timely birth for the euro, and at the same time worried about making the grade itself.
The concern was not that EMU would be delayed -- the cause of speculatation at the beginning of this year -- but that Germany's difficulties would lead to a broader EMU and a weak single currency.

"It seems to me that ... the pro-EMU forces in the government are strengthening," said Thomas Mayer, senior economist at Goldman Sachs in Frankfurt. "And that is not necessarily a good thing for Bunds."
WestLB's Butler said only political horse trading could now ensure a sturdy euro in 1999 with a small group of so-called "hard currency" nations involved.

"Now that Germany has admitted this, there is no longer a way to exclude certain contries based in the criteria alone," he said. "As a result, the only way that Italy, Spain and others can be kept out of the first round is a political deal -- and one that will demand a price."
